title: Time-independent counterdiabatic driving for emergent two-level subspaces in many-body systems
abstract: We show that geodesic motion in the Riemannian manifold of quantum states provides a direct route to time-independent counterdiabatic driving. Using the relation between the counterdiabatic Hamiltonian and the quantum metric tensor, we prove that a constant-speed geodesic makes the Hilbert-Schmidt norm of the counterdiabatic Hamiltonian constant. For effective two-level systems whose counterdiabatic correction has a fixed operator direction, this further implies that the full counterdiabatic Hamiltonian itself is time independent. We illustrate this result with the Landau-Zener model, three-level Stimulated Raman adiabatic passage and a collectively driven Rydberg ensemble in the blockade regime. Limitations of this approach in realistic many-body systems are discussed, where the two-level reduction is only emergent and leakage out of the effective subspace bounds the achievable speedup. In all cases, time-independent counterdiabatic driving achieves unit-fidelity state preparation on timescales substantially shorter than conventional adiabatic protocols while replacing temporally shaped auxiliary controls by fixed-amplitude fields.
summary: The paper develops a theoretical framework showing that following geodesic paths on the quantum state manifold naturally leads to constant counterdiabatic driving. This allows for the design of fast, high-fidelity quantum control protocols using time-independent auxiliary fields, which is demonstrated successfully across models ranging from simple two-level systems to complex Rydberg ensembles.
main_problem: The primary challenge is achieving high-fidelity quantum state preparation on timescales much shorter than conventional adiabatic protocols.
main_result: Geodesic motion in the quantum state manifold allows for the construction of a time-independent counterdiabatic Hamiltonian, enabling fast, high-fidelity control.
method: The authors utilize Riemannian geometry by relating the required counterdiabatic Hamiltonian norm to the quantum metric tensor along geodesic paths in the parameter space.
model_or_system: The theory is illustrated using several models: the Landau-Zener model, three-level STIRAP, and a Rydberg ensemble operating in the blockade regime. These systems are used to demonstrate the principle of constant counterdiabatic driving.
key_observables: Final state fidelity ($F_{GS}(T)$), the norm of the counterdiabatic Hamiltonian ($\|	ext{H}_{	ext{CD}}\|$), and protocol duration ($T$).
important_parameters: The blockade interaction strength ($V$), Rabi frequencies ($\Omega$), detunings ($\Delta$), and the geometric length scale ($\ell_{	ext{geo}}$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the system dynamics can be effectively reduced to a two-level subspace, and that following a geodesic path minimizes the required control effort.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate how geodesic driving maintains a constant norm for $	ext{H}_{	ext{CD}}$ compared to other protocols. They show unit fidelity achieved with time-independent cCD in Landau-Zener, STIRAP, and Rydberg blockade systems over various timescales.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the geometric connection between geodesics and constant $\|	ext{H}_{	ext{CD}}\|$. It then applies this framework to specific physical models (LZ, STIRAP, Rydberg) to demonstrate that time-independent cCD achieves fast, high-fidelity state preparation. Finally, it discusses limitations related to subspace leakage.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful geometric tool for designing quantum control pulses, moving beyond simple time-dependent shaping by showing how fundamental principles (geodesics) can enforce simplicity (time-independent controls) while maintaining speed and fidelity in complex many-body settings.

In contrast, arbitrary protocols experience a parameter-dependent quantum metric, causing the required counterdiabatic field to become stronger in regions where the energy gap is small.
